DEEPGRID SEMI PVT LTD - PRELIMINARY DATASHEET
DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet
Lockstep RISC-V motor-control SoC on SkyWater sky130A, in a 64-pin QFN. Dual rv32imc cores with a fault
comparator, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB self-boot ROM and QSPI-XIP, a 3-phase motor peripheral set (PWM, DShot,
encoder, CORDIC, on-die SAR ADC) and UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers.

Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design
targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The
flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Dual DGridRiscV rv32imc cores in lockstep with a cycle-by-cycle fault comparator and a sticky fault CSR.
• 32 KB on-chip SRAM (no ECC); 64 KB baked boot ROM; QSPI execute-in-place window for external NOR flash.
• 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM with programmable dead-time and a hardware brake.
• 4-channel DShot ESC engine, pin-muxed onto the PWM output pads.
• Quadrature + Hall encoder with edge timestamps; CORDIC (sin/cos, atan2, magnitude) for field-oriented control.
• On-die 8-bit differential SAR ADC for phase-current feedback, PWM-triggered.
• Two UARTs, an SPI master, a 7-bit I2C master, 14-pin GPIO, two timers, a windowed watchdog and rail supervisor.
• Interrupt controller; standalone self-boot (no management core); SLVERR on any unmapped access.
• Single 50 MHz clock domain; whole die powered from a 1.8 V rail; 3.3 V I/O.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. The DG32-LITE die runs entirely from this one 50 MHz domain.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
JTAG idles safely with no probe. TMS (pin 25) and TDI (pin 26) are weakly pulled up on die, TCK (pin 24) weakly pulled down, so
an unconnected JTAG header will not disturb the part.

DEEPGRID SEMI PVT LTD - PRELIMINARY DATASHEET
DG32-2DOM - Preliminary Datasheet
The DG32-LITE motor-control SoC plus an INT8 attention accelerator on a second clock. Same lockstep core, boot
path and motor peripheral set; adds a memory-mapped attention engine (0xE000_0000) that runs on clk_fast_i and
reaches memory through clock-domain-crossing bridges. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers.
Part
Package
Process
Core
Clocks
DG32-2DOM
QFN-64, 9x9 mm
sky130A 130 nm
2x rv32imc + INT8 attn
50 / 114 MHz
Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design
targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The
flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Everything in DG32-LITE: dual rv32imc lockstep core, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB boot ROM, QSPI-XIP, and the full motor
peripheral set (PWM, DShot, encoder, CORDIC, SAR ADC) plus UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO.
• INT8 attention accelerator (0xE000_0000): one kick computes a band of query rows of one head end to end (QK^T,
softmax/EXP, E.V, requantise to int8), bit-exact to the golden model.
• Attention datapath: shared LANES-wide MAC array, 256-entry u15 EXP table, 40-bit numerator (exact to NK=131072),
one reciprocal per row; ~3242 cycles/row analytic at LANES=16.
• Second clock domain: the engine runs on clk_fast_i (114 MHz) and crosses to the 50 MHz CPU domain through 2-flop
CDC bridges, so it never stalls the frozen control core.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. DG32-2DOM adds a second clock, clk_fast_i (114 MHz), for the attention engine; the CPU
and all peripherals stay in the 50 MHz domain and the two are bridged by CDC logic.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
• The attention engine adds no board signals; budget for clk_fast_i only if the CI2612 die brings it out to a pad rather
than deriving it on-die.

flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Everything in DG32-LITE: dual rv32imc lockstep core, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB boot ROM, QSPI-XIP, and the full motor
peripheral set (PWM, DShot, encoder, CORDIC, SAR ADC) plus UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO.
• INT8 attention accelerator (0xE000_0000): one kick computes a band of query rows of one head end to end (QK^T,
softmax/EXP, E.V, requantise to int8), bit-exact to the golden model.
• Attention datapath: shared LANES-wide MAC array, 256-entry u15 EXP table, 40-bit numerator (exact to NK=131072),
one reciprocal per row; ~3242 cycles/row analytic at LANES=16.
• Second clock domain: the engine runs on clk_fast_i (114 MHz) and crosses to the 50 MHz CPU domain through 2-flop
CDC bridges, so it never stalls the frozen control core.
• Own die (3400 x 4500 um) with the attention K/V buffers on sky130 SRAM macros next to the SAR analog corner.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. DG32-2DOM adds a second clock, clk_fast_i (114 MHz), for the attention engine; the CPU
and all peripherals stay in the 50 MHz domain and the two are bridged by CDC logic.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
• The attention engine adds no board signals; budget for clk_fast_i only if the CI2612 die brings it out to a pad rather

Why the ROM is baked logic, not a macro. The macro-map step only rewrites blackboxes; a real ROM definition
survives it, which keeps the OpenFrame-correct non-volatile boot path intact. Deepening it from 4 KB to 16 KB was
measured as effectively free.
Why standalone matters. OpenFrame has nothing else to start the chip. The boot ROM runs the UART banner, reads the
flash header (magic 0xD632_B007) through the 0x1 window, copies the image into SRAM, and jumps to it - all with no
management core.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the private boot ROM alone; the 0x1 XIP window and
SRAM are reachable by loads and stores, not by fetch. Code does not execute in place from external NOR - it is copied to
SRAM first and run from there.

6.3 FPGA bring-up boot - follows Kaushik's SoC4
Booting on FPGA is the same as Kaushik's SoC4 version. The Arty A7-100T bring-up boot sequence is not re-invented for

and with a QSPI NOR on the Pmod header the ROM boots the flash image exactly as on silicon.

11 Application: AVIP bearing-fault detection
The DG32-2DOM attention engine exists to run models like AVIP, an INT8 bearing-fault classifier (dgrid-a8w8). AVIP is
multimodal - a time branch and an FFT branch, each a small conv stack plus a gated recurrent cell - fused by two
self-attention blocks and one cross-attention block, ending in a per-class head. Those attention blocks are exactly what the
engine accelerates. The shipped CWRU-trained model is 47,076 parameters at 94-95% held-out-load accuracy with INT8
equal to FP32; the full AVIP topology is 478,277 parameters. Both map onto the same op set with no new RTL.

chunks.section: 0 2  ·  A L G O R I T H M  C H O I C E
chunks.text:
0 2  ·  A L G O R I T H M  C H O I C E
Where a scalar core is strong
The absence of a MAC array reverses the usual ranking. Comparisons and table lookups cost almost nothing here.
Tree ensembles are the best accuracy per cycle on this part
A 100-tree random forest at depth 8 is roughly 800 comparisons and no
multiplies at all — 0.06 ms, supporting rates above 1 kHz. A neural network
of comparable accuracy on bearing-fault or power-quality classification costs
50–500× more cycles.
This is not a compromise made for the hardware. On the CWRU bearing
benchmark a random forest over five time-domain features reaches 95.6 %,
and cutting from nine features to five costs 0.1 %. A review of 42 papers
finds SVM at 95–100 % against deep methods at 97–100 % — statistically
indistinguishable.
Model capacity is not the bottleneck on these tasks. Signal
conditioning is.
The ordering that follows
First choice — tree ensembles, linear discriminants, PCA with Hotelling T²,
Mahalanobis distance. Sub-millisecond, kHz-capable, inspectable in the field.
Second choice — small dense networks and autoencoders, where a
nonlinear boundary genuinely earns its place. Still sub-millisecond.
Reach for last — recurrent and convolutional models. A GRU at 2.95 ms and
a 1D-CNN at 10.3 ms both fit, but only where the raw waveform carries
something hand-built features miss.
Design rule. Spend effort on band selection, envelope demodulation and
operating-condition normalisation before spending it on model capacity.

Why this matters more than the model
A published feature-ranking study across twelve features found demodulated
features evaluated at the known fault frequency outrank raw statistical
moments by a factor of 4–5. Hilbert-Huang amplitude at the outer-race
frequency scored 225.9; peak-to-peak scored 51.8.
That is the whole argument for spending cycles on envelope demodulation
and band selection rather than on a larger classifier. The envelope chain is
also cheap: band-pass, rectify, low-pass, decimate to 1–2 kS/s, then a modest
FFT. Do the decimation before buffering and the working set never exceeds a
few kB.

chunks.section: 0 9  ·  C O N S T R A I N T
chunks.text:
0 9  ·  C O N S T R A I N T
What the sensing supports
Compute is not the binding constraint on these thirty use cases. The analog front end is.
The current-based use cases need more than 8 bits
ISO 13373-2 gives usable dynamic range as D = 6(N−1) dB, so eight bits yields 42 dB. ISO 20958 states rotor-bar sidebands sit 100 to
1,000 times below the fundamental — −40 to −60 dBc. The entire diagnostic range sits at or below the quantisation floor. Broken rotor bar,
eccentricity and inter-turn short detection need either analog fundamental suppression and gain ahead of the converter, or 12–16 bits.
A second constraint compounds it. Sideband separation is 2·s·f₁ — roughly 3 Hz at full load, 0.5 Hz at light load — so these use cases need
30–100 second records at stable load and speed with 0.01–0.05 Hz resolution. A 2²⁰-point FFT is 8 MB and does not fit. Use Goertzel
evaluated at the predicted sideband frequencies, which is why the electrical use cases on slide 06 are costed that way and not with an FFT.
Tier 1 — one accelerometer
The highest-value addition. Bearings are 44 % of
motor failures and are the weakest fault class
for current-only sensing; rotor bars, where
current is strongest, are 8–10 %. Needs ≥5 kHz
usable bandwidth — many low-cost MEMS
parts roll off at 1–3 kHz, below the bearing
resonance band, which makes envelope analysis
useless. Mounting matters as much as the part:
stud mounting per ISO 13373-1, not magnet or
adhesive.
Tier 2 — three-phase current and voltage
Unlocks negative-sequence detection of stator
inter-turn shorts, instantaneous power signature
analysis and Park's vector per ISO 20958 Annex
A. Needs a multi-channel converter; the part
currently has one differential channel.
What works today, unchanged
Everything on slide 08 and most of slide 09 —

A P P E N D I X
Basis
Read this before quoting any figure elsewhere.
From the design
Core configuration, memory sizes, peripheral set
and the CORDIC capability come from the DG32-
LITE block diagrams dated 10 September 2026
and the consolidated capability assessment of
11 September 2026. The 16.5 KB and 29.5 KB
model budgets and the 12.5 MMAC/s scalar rate
are taken from that assessment.
Derived
Every latency, memory figure and maximum
rate in this deck is calculated — feature-
extraction cycles plus model cycles at 4 cycles
per int8 multiply-accumulate, against 82 % of a
50 MHz core. That constant is back-solved
from the design documents and has not
been measured on silicon. One cycle-
accurate measurement on run R firmware
relocates every rate here.
Third-party, verified 11 Sept 2026
CWRU random-forest accuracy and the 42-paper
review, the twelve-feature ranking study, the
kurtosis non-monotonicity result, and the ISO
signal-processing limits were checked against
primary sources — IEEE and MDPI papers, the
PHM Society proceedings, and the ISO catalogue
entries for 13373-1, 13373-2, 20958 and 20816-
3.
On accuracy expectations
Do not carry published bearing-benchmark accuracy into a specification.
Forty of forty-one reviewed CWRU studies used splits vulnerable to data
leakage; on a leakage-free bearing-wise split one classifier fell from 85.8 % to
69.5 %. Realistic accuracy on unseen physical bearings is 65–80 %. Smith
and Randall further showed a meaningful fraction of CWRU records are not
diagnosable by correct physics at all, which is why 99 % figures on that
dataset should be treated as artefacts.
What is not claimed
No workload here has been compiled for or measured on DG32-LITE, which
has not completed place-and-route. No inference result carries a safety
integri

Lockstep RISC-V motor-control SoC on SkyWater sky130A, in a 64-pin QFN. Dual rv32imc cores with a fault
comparator, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB self-boot ROM and QSPI-XIP, a 3-phase motor peripheral set (PWM, DShot,
encoder, CORDIC, on-die SAR ADC) and UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers.

Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design
targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The
flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Dual DGridRiscV rv32imc cores in lockstep with a cycle-by-cycle fault comparator and a sticky fault CSR.
• 32 KB on-chip SRAM (no ECC); 64 KB baked boot ROM; QSPI execute-in-place window for external NOR flash.
• 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM with programmable dead-time and a hardware brake.
• 4-channel DShot ESC engine, pin-muxed onto the PWM output pads.
• Quadrature + Hall encoder with edge timestamps; CORDIC (sin/cos, atan2, magnitude) for field-oriented control.
• On-die 8-bit differential SAR ADC for phase-current feedback, PWM-triggered.
• Two UARTs, an SPI master, a 7-bit I2C master, 14-pin GPIO, two timers, a windowed watchdog and rail supervisor.
• Interrupt controller; standalone self-boot (no management core); SLVERR on any unmapped access.
• Single 50 MHz clock domain; whole die powered from a 1.8 V rail; 3.3 V I/O.

6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. The DG32-LITE die runs entirely from this one 50 MHz domain.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
JTAG idles safely with no probe. TMS (pin 25) and TDI (pin 26) are weakly pulled up on die, TCK (pin 24) weakly pulled down, so
an unconnected JTAG header will not disturb the part.

1. Why firmware cannot do this (confirming Ayaz's argument)
DShot600 is 1.67 µs/bit; the 0/1 decision is a high-time of 625 ns vs 1250 ns. At 50 MHz that is
31 vs 62 cycles, so the decode needs ~±15-cycle (±300 ns) edge placement — achievable only
by a busy-wait loop with interrupts off for

the lockstep compare window — dgrid_lockstep_check  compares every committed
store; a firmware bit-bang that branches on pad reads produces store streams whose
timing depends on an asynchronous input, which is exactly the class of behaviour the
checker is designed to flag.
And bidirectional reply is impossible in firmware regardless of speed: the ESC must turn
the pad from input to output ~30 µs after the command frame ends and drive a 21-bit reply —
the pad has no output-enable today. This is a pad-ring fact, not a software one.
Conclusion: hardware RX + hardware reply, or no ESC role.
2. What exists today (baseline)
dgrid_dshot  (slot 0xC, rtl/dgrid_dshot.sv ) is transmit-only: 4 channels, one shared bit-time
counter, per-channel 16-bit frame + CRC4, programmable BITPERIOD / T0H / T1H . Its only pins
are output [3:0] dshot_o . The four channels reach the pads only through SYSCTL PINMUX[0] ,
which AND-ORs them onto the PWM high-side pads AH / BH / CH / SAMPLE_TRIG
( dg32_lite_top.sv:775-792 ). The low-side PWM pads are never muxed, so a mis-set mux cannot
shoot through a bridge.
Pad budget is 44/44 with zero spare. There is no pad for a receiver. The RX path therefore
must reuse the same four pads, which means those pads become bidirectional. That is the
single most consequential change in this spec (§7).
3. Protocol facts the design depends on

pulse of fixed period; high-time encodes the value (long = 1, short = 0).

chunks.text:
3.3 Telemetry reply (ESC → FC), what the reply engine sends
The reply is not a DShot command frame, so it cannot reuse the TX engine's shifter
unmodified:
1. Payload: 16 bits = [15:4]  eRPM period (3-bit exponent e , 9-bit mantissa m ; period_µs = m
<< e ) · [3:0]  CRC where crc = ~(v ^ v>>4 ^ v>>8) & 0xF  over the 12-bit period field.
2. GCR 4b→5b encode each nibble (table: 19 1B 12 13 1D 15 16 17 1A 09 0A 0B 1E 0D 0E 0F )
→ 20 bits.
3. Transition-encode to 21 bits: out[0] = 0; out[i] = out[i-1] ^ G[i-1]  — a 1  in the GCR
stream is a level transition, not a level.
4. Transmit inverted, at 5/4 the command bit rate (DShot600 → 750 kbit/s, 1.33 µs/bit =
66.7 cycles), starting ~30 µs after the command frame's last edge.
The FC decodes edges back with G = s ^ (s >> 1) . This is the Betaflight/Bluejay/AM32
convention; get any of the three steps wrong and every FC on the market reports CRC errors.
4. Architecture
Recommendation: extend slot 0xC in place, not a new slot. The RX and reply engines are
added inside dgrid_dshot  as two self-contained sub-modules ( dgrid_dshot_rx , dgrid_dshot_tel ),
sharing the existing AXI slave, the pad mux and the bit-timing registers. Reasons: (a) the
address map has no free slot without touching the decoder and error-slave logic that is frozen for
tape-in; (b) RX and TX are mutually exclusive on the same pads, so one owner of the pad
direction is safer than two; (c) BITPERIOD/T0H/T1H  already encode the speed class — RX derives
its threshold from them by default.
                       ┌───────────── dgrid_dshot (slot 0xC) ─────────────┐
   AXI-lite ──────────►│ regs │ TX engine (existing) ───────────┐          │
                       │      │                                  │ mux/dir │──► pad_o[3:0]
                       │      │ dgrid_d

Synchroniser + filter add a fixed 3-cycle (60 ns) latency to both edges, so measured width
is unaffected.
4.2 Reply engine dgrid_dshot_tel  (per channel)
Armed when TELEM_EN=1  and a valid frame with telem=1  arrives (or TELEM_ALWAYS=1  —
bidirectional FCs expect a reply on every frame).
Waits TURNAROUND  cycles from the command frame's last edge, then asserts pad_oe , drives
the 21-bit stream from TELEMn  at TELEMPERIOD  cycles/bit (inverted), then releases pad_oe
and returns the pad to input.
GCR + transition encoding (§3.3) done in hardware from the 12-bit period value firmware
writes to TELEMn . Firmware supplies only {e, m} ; CRC, GCR and transition coding are
hardware. This keeps the firmware side to one register write per commutation-period
update.
If a new command frame's first edge arrives while a reply is being driven, the reply is
aborted and OE released within one cycle — never fight the FC for the wire. TEL_ABORT
status bit is set.
4.3 Direction ownership
pad_oe  per channel is the OR of: TX engine BUSY  (existing TX role, always drives) and
dgrid_dshot_tel  driving . In RX-only or RX+reply roles the TX engine is never started, so the pad
idles as input. PINMUX[0]  continues to select DShot vs PWM; PWM-role pads remain output-
only (OE forced high) so the bridge-safety property is preserved.

Note on clearing VALID : W1C is the safe default and matches the other DG32 peripherals.

6. Interrupts
One new source into dgrid_irq  (0xDF): dshot_rx_irq = (IRQ_FRAME_EN & |VALID) | (IRQ_ERR_EN &
|(CRC_ERR|OVERRUN|TEL_ABORT)) . Level, cleared by W1C of the underlying flags. dgrid_irq  has a
16-bit raw vector with bits 0–6 and 8 (attention, 2dom) used; bit 7 is 1'b0  today and is the
natural slot ( rtl/dgrid_irq.sv:58 ). Bits 9–15 are also free. Follow the existing convention: add
dshot_rx_i = 1'b0  as a defaulted port so the frozen lite netlist is unchanged when the port is left
unconnected — and tie it explicitly in the top (sv2v drops port defaults).
7. Pad-ring change — the real cost of this feature

constant drive (lines 408–414).

India buys almost every one of its simpler chips from other countries. About $9 billion of them

PART ONE
India buys almost every one of these chips from abroad Nobody in India makes them. The reason
is money, not skill. And money can be changed.
1 What India buys, and why nobody here makes it
Start with one number. Last year India imported $23.4 billion of chips. That figure is from UN
COMTRADE, code HS 8542. It is the only number in this section that comes from outside our
company. About 70 % of it came from China and Taiwan. Inside that total, analysts estimate
about $9 billion a year is the kind of chip this document is about. These are chips made on
older, larger factory processes — 130 nanometres and above. Power management chips. Small
microcontrollers. Motor gate drivers. Data-line transceivers. Voltage supervisors. Electricity-
meter front ends. These are not exciting chips. But they are most of the chips in any product. A
car has one or two advanced processors and several dozen of these older ones. A smart electricity
meter has none of the advanced kind at all. So the import bill is large, and it stays large.
DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad

Figure 1 is a funnel, not a headline. Each step down makes the number smaller and makes it more
believable. Walk down it:
• $23.4 bn to $9 bn. We cut out chips made on newer, smaller processes. We do not build those.
This
divides the number by 2.6.
• $9 bn to $0.46 bn. We cut down to the nine kinds of chip we actually build. This is the biggest
cut, a
factor of 19.
• $0.46 bn to ₹1,000 Cr. This is what we think we can sell by FY31.
• ₹1,000 Cr to ₹2.88 Cr. This is what we have already sold. A factor of 35.
We would rather you argue with the bottom number than believe the top one.
1.1 Why has nobody in India filled this gap?
India has plenty of chip designers. So why is the gap still there? The answer is not skill. It is a
fixed cost. Designing a chip the normal way costs $2 million to $5 million before you sell a single
unit. Most of that is not design work. It is:
• physical layout work sent to an outside company: $1–2 million per chip
• software licences for design tools: $0.5–1 million every year
• a full set of photographic masks to print the chip: $0.5–1 million
To pay that back you need volume.
Millions of units, over several years, selling to a market
that does not change its mind. Now look at what Indian defence and industry actually ask for. A
power management chip for one avionics box might sell 10,000 units a year. It needs a specification
nobody else uses. It must be screened to a military standard. You cannot build that chip against
a $2–5 million setup cost. Not because it is hard. Because the sums do not work. So the big chip
companies do the only sensible thing. They offer a catalogue chip with the wrong specification, or
an old chip that is about to

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
development money. This combination is unusual, and it matters more than the market size. In a
normal market, a cheap new competitor is answered with a price cut. Here, once an item is on a
PIL, the foreign supplier cannot be chosen at any price. And once we are on an approved-vendor
list, it becomes expensive for the customer to switch away from us. There is one catch in this
argument. It is big enough that we will raise it ourselves.
BUY(INDIAN) IS NOT THE SAME AS BUY(INDIAN-IDDM), AND FOR NOW WE ARE THE
FIRST ONE The IDDM category depends on how much of the product’s value is Indian. It does
not depend on where the design was done. Our first chips will be made in a factory in Wisconsin
in the USA, and the radar chip in Germany. The design, the circuit code, the verification and the
layout are all Indian. The silicon wafer is not. Read strictly, that probably puts us in Buy(Indian)
and not Buy(Indian-IDDM), until we are making chips at SCL Mohali in India. Two things follow.
First, Buy(Indian) still beats a straight import, and a PIL removes the import whichever category
we are in. So the advantage is real. It is just one step lower than the strongest version of this
argument. Second, this makes the SCL Mohali factory a business need, not a nice-tohave. That
is why we keep it in the plan even though it is the least proven of our three factories.
1.3 Why now, and not five years ago
Nothing above is new information. The import problem has been visible for thirty years. The
engineering talent has been here for twenty. Four things changed recently, and all four had to
change: Free chip design kits became real. A factory design kit, or PDK, is the file set you need
to d

PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
PART TWO
We changed the cost, and we have real chips to prove it Our cost per finished chip is about ten
times lower. Not because we are clever. Because four bills are not on our list.
2 Our costs, line by line
Our claim is small and easy to test: Use an older factory process, a free design kit and an
automated design flow.
Together these cut the cost of a finished, tested, low-volume chip by
about ten times. This makes a group of chips profitable that the big companies cannot profitably
make. Indian law then keeps the customer with us for a decade.
The important word is cannot. We are not saying we are cleverer than Texas Instruments. We
are saying four bills on their list are not on ours. That changes which order sizes make money.
Cost item Normal chip company Our way Physical layout $1–2 M sent outside, per chip done
in-house on free kits — staff time only Design tool licences $0.5–1 M every year free tools —
almost nothing Design time 12–18 months per chip design files in under 30 days; chips every 180
days Prototype masks $0.5–1 M for a full set shared factory run — ₹14.3 L on sky130, ₹34–80
L on IHP Testing and approval rolled into the project cost ₹40–80 L per chip, listed separately
Total per chip $2–5 M ₹0.6–1.2 Cr including approval Three of those numbers are now quoted
from the supplier’s own price page, and one of them shows we were wrong. A shared factory run
on sky130 costs $14,950. That is ₹14.3 L at today’s rate. It returns 100 finished, packaged chips,
and gives you about 15 mm² of space on the shared die. We had been saying ₹15–40 L per chip.
So for nine of our ten chips we were charging ourselves too much. The tenth one goes the other
way. The rada

PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
Every tool in the middle of Figure 2 is free software running on our own computers. Yosys for logic.
OpenROAD for layout. TritonCTS for the clock network. TritonRoute for wiring. OpenRCX for
extraction. Magic and KLayout for final checks. Four of the rows in the table above are an invoice
for a normal chip company. For us they are staff time. So one more design attempt costs us
almost nothing. That single fact is what lets a small company build a range of chips instead of
one.
2.1 What this does and does not mean
It does not mean we can beat a mass-market chip at ten million units. At that volume the big
company has already paid off its setup cost, and it buys wafers cheaper than we do. We would
lose. Saying otherwise would be the fastest way to lose your trust. What it means is this. A
chip selling 10,000 units a year is a product for us. It is not a product for Texas Instruments. At
₹0.6–1.2 Cr total we can build it, get it approved, and sell it at 60–75 % gross margin. And in
this market, the law stops the big company being chosen anyway. This is a low-end entry into a
protected market. It is a known strategy with a known way of failing, and §12 deals with that
failure directly instead of ignoring it. An argument about cost only matters if the method has
actually made a chip. It has.
3 What we have already made
Read this section differently from the rest. Nothing here is a forecast. A 130 nm test chip, made at
SkyWater using our own automated flow. This is the key proof. It means our software produced a
real design file, a real factory accepted it, and real working silicon came back. Our floating-point
maths work at 130 nm is on that chip. Every speed and cost cla

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
Figure 3. Done, next, and still unproven, in three clearly different colours so nobody reading quickly
can confuse them.
3.1 One number people misread, and one that is genuinely open
81.25 MHz is a limit of the FPGA, not of our design. It took eighteen builds to get the Artix-7
prototype working at that speed with the maths engines included. That proves the circuit code
is correct and can be built. It says nothing about the real chip. The product is a 130 nm chip
running at a fixed 200 MHz. We would rather explain this once, here, than have it read later as
a performance claim. Which brings us to the one open item we would raise if we were reading
this document. THE BIGGEST UNPROVEN CLAIM IN THIS DOCUMENT We say our chips
run at 200 MHz. We have not yet published the timing analysis that proves it, and it is not clear
which factory kit that analysis was run against. Running that analysis on sky130 and publishing
the report is action 2 of seven in §14. It is the cheapest credibility we can buy. We are putting
this here, in the evidence section, because that is where a reader would look for it. Cost and real
silicon are the two halves of the claim. The next question an engineer asks is whether 130 nm is
a real engineering choice or just the cheap option.
DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad
13

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
PART THREE
The machine: this process, this loop, this library 130 nm is the right process for these chips for
reasons of physics, not price. The loop that turns that into a range of products runs every 198
days. And what builds up over time is not the chips. It is the library underneath them.
4 Why 130 nm is the right process, not the cheap one
In chips, people assume newer is better. For this kind of chip that is simply wrong, and the reasons
are physical. High voltage works here. 130 nm and 180 nm factory processes offer thick-oxide
transistors and LDMOS devices. These handle 5 volts up to 120 volts directly. So a 28 V aircraft
power rail, a 120 V motor supply and a 0.9 V digital core can all sit on one chip. On a newer,
smaller process the power circuits move back onto the circuit board as separate parts. That is the
opposite of what you want. More board space, more parts to buy, more things to fail. This is why
four of our ten chips exist at all. Chip 1 has a 5–120 V converter next to a 200 MHz processor.
Chip 3 puts an aircraft-standard input stage, an LDMOS power stage and four power rails on one
chip. Chip 5 needs a 5 V-tolerant output ring. Chip 8 drives 0–12 V into a display panel across
3,840 outputs. None of these can be made on a newer process at any price. Radiation resistance
comes from size. A cosmic ray can flip a stored bit. The bigger the transistor, the more charge
is needed to flip it, so bigger transistors are harder to disturb. Protection methods such as DICE
latches and triple redundancy cost chip area, and area is the one thing an older process has spare.
On chip 3 the power sequencer uses triple redundancy and DICE latches, and this costs a f

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
from a temperature-corrected reference circuit and closely matched resistors. For chip 5 the argu-
ment reverses completely. A newer process is actively worse for a line driver. A line driver needs
a 5 V-tolerant thick output ring with strong static-discharge protection. Newer processes do not
have one. This is why interface chips from every major company are still made on older processes
today. One place the process is a hard limit. Chip 7 is a 4D radar front end. It cannot be built on
ordinary CMOS. The sky130 process will not reach 77 GHz. Not slowly, not expensively. Not at
all. The IHP SG13G2 process is a 130 nm SiGe process with special high-speed transistors that
reach about 350 GHz. This is the transistor type that real 77 GHz car radar uses. So the design
splits into two chips, one on each process, with the boundary at the analogue-to-digital converter.
One result of this belongs here and not in a footnote. You cannot prototype a 77 GHz front end on
an FPGA. FPGA testing covers the digital half only. The high-frequency half is proven in silicon
or not at all. AND ONE PLACE WHERE A FREE DESIGN KIT IS A PROBLEM, NOT A
BENEFIT Everything above is true of the factory process. It is not yet true of the parts library. A
paid 130 nm design kit comes with a tested library of analogue building blocks: reference circuits,
protection cells rated to a stated level, memory. A free kit does not. So the ±15 kV protection
ring on chip 5, the temperature-stable reference on chip 3 and the memory on chip 1 are targets
with no tested example to copy. We have to build and prove each one in silicon before it becomes
a datasheet number. That is real work and real schedule. It is

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
Figure 4. The process plan. 130 and 180 nm now. A move to 90, 55 and 45 nm from 2028, where
the limit is the number of channels rather than the clock speed. 28 nm from 2030. The panel also
corrects an arithmetic mistake in an earlier internal draft, because that draft’s ”1,000 chips” and
”10 per year” could not both be true.
The process is right and the cost is right. What turns those two facts into a range of products,
rather than one product, is the loop.
5 One loop every 198 days
Progress here is not measured in milestones. It is measured in factory runs. Our hiring plan, our
cash need and how fast the product range grows all follow from how long one run takes, and from
which half of it can be repeated.

chunks.section: Design: 30 days or less. Specification, then circuit code, then verification, then layout, then final
chunks.text:
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
Design: 30 days or less. Specification, then circuit code, then verification, then layout, then final
checks. Verification and circuit code go back and forth with each other. Nothing else in the chain
does. This half is limited by how many engineers we have, and engineers are what money buys.
The manufacturing gate. To go ahead you need enough verification coverage, no timing failures,
and a clean layout check. These are targets today, not history, and the figures say so. Silicon: 168
days. Masks, wafers, packaging, testing. This half cannot be repeated at all. One mistake costs
a whole cycle. That is why we enforce the design-complete gate before the factory window, not
during it. That 168 is not our estimate. It is the gap between sending the design and receiving
packaged chips on the published factory calendar. From 16 September 2026 to 3 March 2027 on
the CI2609 run. From 7 December 2026 to 25 May 2027 on CI2612. We had been saying “about
150 days”, which was a rounded guess. So one full cycle is 30 + 168 = 198 days, not 180. We
would rather correct our own headline than have you find the factory’s calendar and correct it for
us. We keep the name because the design half is the part we control. The arithmetic is in Figure

chunks.section: 6.1 What a shared die can and cannot do
chunks.text:
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base

6.1 What a shared die can and cannot do
TinyTapeout puts hundreds of small designs on one die behind a shared wrapper. Each design
gets a fixed tile of space, and a switch picks which one connects to the shared pins. Only one
design works at a time. That is excellent for what it does, and completely unable to do four
things:
• Space. A tile is about 0.02 mm². That is a few hundred to a few thousand logic gates. A motor
controller
with a power converter, a 16-bit converter, seven output channels and a processor is several mm².
No sellable chip fits in a tile.
• Analogue and high voltage. The wrapper is digital only. No high-voltage devices, no reference
circuits,
no converters, no thick output ring, no high-speed radar transistors. Chips 3, 5, 6, 7 and the
output stage of chip 8 cannot be tested this way at all.
• Using many pins at once. The pins are shared and time-switched. You cannot test 3,840 display
out-
puts, or seven motor channels, or four radar receivers. You can show a digital block works. You
cannot measure noise, power supply rejection, or accuracy across temperature from a tile.
• Datasheet measurements.
6.2 The change of word
The mistake is calling a tile a chip. It is not. It is a building block. And every chip in our range
breaks down into digital building blocks, and those do fit in a tile: the motor control datapath,
the tuning loop, the meter filter, the fault table, the noise filters, the lockstep comparator, the
display timing generator, the network shaper, the encryption cores, the memory controller, the
radar processing control. Do not say “1,000 chips in five years.” A chip means a datasheet, an
approval, a test program and a place on an appr

6.5 Two things we would argue with in our own plan
Custom chip-to-chip connections stop us selling a single die. We chose not to use the UCIe industry
standard. That avoids a real area and power cost, but it means no other company can buy one of
our dies as a component. If selling dies is ever the plan, the connection standard has to be chosen
now. Changing it later is a redesign. Packaging is a supply chain that is not yet in our plan. The
end goal is six chips in one package: power,
motor drive, communications, safety, control and analogue, with the 28 nm AI chip joining later.
This multiplies volume, because one packaged product contains six chips. But it needs an assembly
partner, package-level testing, and an answer to what happens when one chip in six is faulty.
That last question forces you to test every chip before assembly, and §10 carries it as a cost and a
schedule line rather than a detail. One method, one library. The next question is which factories
it runs in, and whether ”works on any process” survives contact with an analogue circuit.

chunks.section: 8.1 Every missing feature is a decision

8.1 Every missing feature is a decision
A reviewer will read the second half of that table as a list of gaps unless we explain each one.
No caches.
A cache is a small fast memory that keeps recently used data.
It usually helps,
but sometimes it misses and then the access takes far longer. These are control chips that must
respond in a guaranteed time. A cache turns a guaranteed worst case into an average, and that
is the wrong trade for a motor loop, a power sequencer or a safety monitor. Our processor goes
straight to closely attached memory with a fixed access time. Chip 1’s hardware control loop
responds in under 1 microsecond, and that number only means something because nothing in the
path can miss. No branch prediction. Same reason, plus chip area. A cost you always pay is easier
to plan for than one you usually avoid. And these control loops are short and dominated by data
processing rather than branching. No floating-point unit. Every calculation in our range uses
fixed-point maths by design. Fixed-point is smaller, faster, and gives exactly the same answer on
every chip. That matters when the same calculation must match between a screened chip and a
commercial one. Our floating-point work at 130 nm sits on the test chip as a separate engine, not
inside the control processor. No compressed instructions. Compressed instructions save memory
space. That matters when instruction memory is off the chip and expensive. Here it is on the chip
and sized to the job, and removing the feature removes an alignment case from the fetch path.
Memory protection instead of a full memory manager. These chips run bare-metal code or a small
realtime operating system. What they ne

10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys
Approval is not one test. For a commercial industrial chip it is a defined sequence with a defined
number of samples. For a screened defence chip it is longer. Characterisation means measuring
the chip across manufacturing variation, voltage and temperature, on enough units to write a
datasheet with real limits instead of simulated ones. Reliability means hightemperature life testing,
temperature cycling, humidity, static-discharge and latch-up testing. And for defence versions,
screening means burn-in, electrical testing at temperature extremes, leak testing on the package
seal, and the paperwork trail that MIL-883, JSS and CEMILAC approval require. The reliability
and screening steps take calendar time. More money does not make them shorter. Five of the
eight steps to a screened chip are in that category. This is why the plan sends commercial chips
first, and pushes chip 6 through the process early — specifically to learn where it slows down
before four other chips are queued behind it. One factory run cannot approve a chip, and that
costs money. A shared run gives you one set of wafers, usually made at typical settings. An
approval needs material from more than one batch, so that batch-tobatch variation is included
in the samples. A defence screening process will ask for it. So ₹40–80 L per chip is honestly a
commercial-grade approval figure. A screened version needs extra material, and for the analogue
chips that means extra factory runs, not just extra test time. We have sized the round for four
approvals rather than seven for exactly this reason, and §13 names the three that are not funded.

11 Two ways to sell the same chip
Selling chips is not a pitch. It is a sequence of things you hand the customer. A design engineer
downloads a datasheet, decides in ten minutes whether the chip can work, buys an evaluation
board with a credit card, gets it running in a week, and only then does anyone discuss commercial
terms. If any item in that chain is missing, the process stops there, no matter how good the silicon
is.

14.1 The seven things we would fix first, in order of value
1. Publish what the 130 nm test chip actually cost, and what was on it. This is the correction
we least wanted and most needed. The whole cost argument in §2 rests on a ₹0.6–1.2 Cr figure
that has never been done once. Except that we have already made a chip on this method, so
a real number exists and we are simply not showing it. It either supports the claim or it does
not, and either way a reader is entitled to it before being asked to trust the estimate. It also
answers the question behind it: did that chip contain any analogue? 2. Run the timing analysis
on sky130 and publish it, per chip. The 200 MHz number is the biggest claim we make and it is
currently a design target. One report per chip turns it into a fact, and it is the cheapest credibility
available to us. 3. Get the production price quote in writing. Our factory service has said it is
willing to support a direct production route. Their published FAQ still says prototypes only. A
quoted mask set and first wafer batch turns the whole production half of this plan from a verbal
indication into a number. That is the difference between a company that can invoice in FY27 and
one that cannot. 4. Get the BEL electronic-warfare specification. It unlocks the highest-value
matches on the government lists, and settles the SiGe-versus-CMOS question that gates the whole
chip 7 family. 5. Replace target numbers with measured numbers. When the first 130 nm batch
comes back, swap in real coverage, timing, yield and test results for the current targets. Every
drawing in this document is built to accept that swap without being redrawn. That one change
turns a plan

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
14.2
Where we could fool ourselves — the audit we ran on our own plan
We checked this plan for wishful thinking using investor Charlie Munger’s famous checklist —
the way we would tear apart somebody else’s pitch. The core survives: the ten-times cost cut is
arithmetic; ₹2.88 crore of orders is fact; the import bans are real. Four kinds of wishful thinking
had crept in, and each one changed this document:
• Borrowed glory. We quoted other companies’ huge order books in ways that made them
sound like our orders. Fixed — they are labelled as the size of the door, and our money moves
only on our own signed letters.
• Permission mistaken for orders. A list entry is permission, not an order. Fixed — the
three buyer speeds in §11.2, each with its own clock.
• Protecting our own number. Our forecast added to exactly ₹1,000 crore in every revision
— a sign we were protecting the number. Fixed — the crash-price table now travels with it
everywhere.
• One skill mistaken for another. Being good at chips is not being good at supporting three
hundred customers. Fixed — the support-engineer team is a funded line.
When everything pushes one way: national pride, government deadlines, finished docu-
ments and exciting tender numbers all push the same direction — build more, faster. When
every force in the room points one way, that is itself the warning. Our defence is the rule, the

chunks.section: DeepGrid DG32-2DOM Silicon Architecture & Attention Variant Specification
chunks.text:
**Document Reference**: DG32-2DOM System Architecture - Block Definition  
**Target Shuttle**: chipIgnite CI2612 · **Foundry & Node**: SkyWater sky130A 130 nm CMOS  
**Die Revision**: `dg32_2dom (A3)` · **Die Dimensions**: 3400 × 4500 µm (15.30 mm²)  
**Process/CPU**: 2× RV32IMC DGridRiscV Lockstep + INT8 Attention Engine  
**Clock Frequencies**: 50 MHz Core Domain (`clk_i`) / 114 MHz Fast Domain (`clk_fast_i`)  
**Classification**: DeepGrid Semi Technical Annex · Confidential Silicon Diligence Canon  

---

The **DG32-2DOM** is the dual-domain attention variant (`INCLUDE_ATTN=1`) of DeepGrid Semi's motor-control SoC family, carried on the chipIgnite CI2612 shuttle. It integrates the hardened, flight-control motor core of the DG32-LITE alongside a dedicated, hardware **INT8 attention engine** operating on a second, asynchronous 114 MHz clock domain (`clk_fast_i`).

Both variants share a unified RTL code tree; DG32-2DOM is instantiated via synthesis defines and clock crossing bridges rather than a separate repository fork.

---

Every subsystem in DG32-2DOM derives from physical silicon findings verified during bring-up:

1. **CPU PMA Whitelist**:
   The VexiiRiscv core enforces a strict hardware whitelist:
   $$\text{fault} = \neg(\text{addr}[31] \ | \ \text{addr}[31:28] == \text{0x1})$$
   Any address that does not set bit 31 or reside in `0x1xxxxxxx` generates a CPU load/store fault before reaching the bus. Placing main SRAM at `0x9000_0000` clears this rule; placing it at `0x2000_0000` results in immediate CPU exception faults.
2. **`ar_addr` Valid Only at Handshake**:
   The decoded AXI slave target is latched strictly at the AR handshake cycle (`arsel_q` / `arsel_v`) and held across the transaction. Live decoding from `ar_addr` misroutes read replies.
3. **Private DMEM for Lockstep Checker Core**:
   The redundant `CHECKER` core utilizes private 16 KB DMEM (8 macros) with outputs discarded. If DMEM were shared, a single physical memory defect could corrupt both cores identically. Because the checker cannot see external peripheral loads, firmware polling on asynchronous pads must be managed within the comparator window.
4. **Standalone OpenFrame Architecture**:
   OpenFrame provides no supervisory management core. The 64 KB baked Boot ROM plus QSPI-XIP NOR flash constitutes the entire boot path. Unmapped bus accesses complete with `SLVERR` to prevent bus hangs from permanently bricking the chip.
5. **Dual-Domain Timing Separation**:
   The lockstep CPU core achieves $f_{\max} \approx 55\text{–}62\text{ MHz}$ post-route on sky130A, setting the 50 MHz target (sign-off over-constrained to 54 MHz). Peripherals easily harden above 167 MHz. To prevent the heavy INT8 attention engine from disturbing the core's timing closure, the engine runs on its own 114 MHz clock (`clk_fast_i`) isolated behind

Decoded via `addr[31:28]` and sub-decoded on the `0xD` page via `addr[27:24]`:

| Base Address | Block Name | Domain | Bus Role & Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `0x1000_0000` | `QSPI-XIP` | 50 MHz | External NOR flash read window for image staging into SRAM. |
| `0x9000_0000` | `SRAM` | 50 MHz | 32 KB main memory (16 macros, 512×32 each); idle port enables contention-free DMA. |
| `0xC000_0000` | `dgrid_dshot` | 50 MHz | 4-channel ESC engine, pad-muxed onto high-side PWM pins. |
| `0xD000_0000` | `UART0` | 50 MHz | 8N1 serial console; carries boot banner (115,200 baud @ 50 MHz = 434 clocks/bit). |
| `0xD100_0000` | `UART1` | 50 MHz | Dedicated telemetry link to companion processor. |
| `0xD200_0000` | `SPI Master` | 50 MHz | Up to 25 MHz full-duplex master SPI; 0.64 µs per 16-bit word. |
| `0xD300_0000` | `GPIO` | 50 MHz | 16-pin general I/O with 2-FF synchronizers and atomic `SET` / `CLR` registers. |
| `0xD400_0000` | `TIMER0` | 50 MHz | General-purpose down-counter for RTOS tick. |
| `0xD500_0000` | `TIMER1` | 50 MHz | General-purpose down-counter for control-loop periods. |
| `0xD600_0000` | `Fault CSR` | 50 MHz | Sticky-first poison latch (`cause 001 = DATA_MISMATCH`); MAGIC `0xDEAD_5AFE` inject. |
| `0xD700_0000` | `Supervisor` | 50 MHz | Windowed watchdog (`WDTMIN` / `WDTMAX`) and power rail deglitch monitor. |
| `0xD800_0000` | `PWM` | 50 MHz | 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM; 5.1 µs dead-time; hardware brake ($\le 2$ cyc). |
| `0xD900_0000` | `I2C Master` | 50 MHz | 7-bit master at 100/400 kHz with clock stretching and true open-drain pad drive. |
| `0xDA00_0000` | `Encoder` | 50 MHz | Decodes quadrature A/B/Z and Hall states; 32-bit free-running timestamp for velocity. |
| `0xDB00_0000` | `SAR ADC` | 50 MHz | 8-bit differential OpenFASO

The attention engine computes $QK^T$, row max, 256-entry u15 EXP, normalization $Z$, and $E \cdot V$ projection:

1. **Why INT8 Replaced INT4**:
   In early INT4 evaluations with $N_K \approx 400$ keys, uniform softmax weights ($\frac{1}{400} = 0.0025$) rounded identically to zero, causing mathematical collapse. The INT8 engine retains full **unsigned 15-bit integers (`u15`)** across the softmax pipeline, accumulating into a **40-bit signed numerator seat**.
2. **Why a 40-Bit Numerator is Required**:
   Standard 32-bit signed integers overflow at $2^{31}-1$, failing at $N_K = 512$. A 40-bit accumulator provides exact precision up to $N_K = 131,072$ keys.
3. **Hardware Division**:
   A dedicated 48-step restoring divider calculates the per-row reciprocal $\frac{1}{Z}$.
4. **On-Chip Buffer Residency**:
   K and V buffers are mapped to dedicated on-chip sky130 SRAM macros loaded once per kick via DMA. Re-reading locally per query row reduces bus traffic by **400×**, limiting bus occupancy to ~1%.
5. **Analytic Cycle Cost**:
   $$\text{Cycles per query row} = \frac{N_K \cdot K_D}{\text{LANES}} + \frac{N_K \cdot D_V}{\text{LANES}} + 48 + 11 \cdot D_V + \text{writeback} + \text{drain}$$
   At $\text{LANES}=16, K_D=32, D_V=64, N_K=400$, execution requires **3,242 cycles per row on `clk_fast_i` (114 MHz)**.

---

All cycle counts are measured on the sky130A post-route silicon:
- **Phase Current Sampling**: On-die SAR ADC triggered at ripple null = **177 cycles** (~3.54 µs). Replaces ~1.9 µs external SPI read.
- **Clarke / Park Transform**: Hardware CORDIC = **53–58 cycles**.
- **PI Regulators**: VexiiRiscv CPU = **~8 cycles / instruction** (fetch-bound, int8 MAC takes 54 cycles vs 6 with I-cache).
- **Inverse Park Transform**: Hardware CORDIC = **53–58 cycles**.
- **Fixed Hardware Overhead**: $\approx \mathbf{300\text{ cycles}}$ (~6 µs).
- **Headroom at 10 kHz (5,000 cycles @ 50 MHz)**: Leaves **~4,700 cycles (>90% headroom)** for state observers, thermal models, and serial communication.
- **Closed-Loop Bandwidth**: ~5 µs acquisition + ~5 µs compute = **~100 kHz closed-loop control capability**.

---

chunks.section: 5. Physical Silicon Area Breakdown (15.30 mm² Die)
chunks.text:
Measured via Yosys synthesis against `sky130_fd_sc_hd` and LEF footprints:
- **Total Die Dimensions**: 3400 × 4500 µm = **15.30 mm²**.
- **Placed Cell + Macro Footprint**: **5.93 mm²**.
- **Standard-Cell Logic Subtotal**: **0.751 mm²** (CPU cores 0.33 mm², Attention logic 0.07 mm², Comparator 0.04 mm², CORDIC 0.02 mm²).
- **Hard Macros Subtotal**: **5.177 mm² (86% of placed area!)**:
  - 16× Main 2 KB SRAM macros: $4.5527\text{ mm}^2$.
  - Attention K buffer macro: $0.2845\text{ mm}^2$.
  - Attention V buffer macro: $0.2845\text{ mm}^2$.
  - SAR ADC macro: $0.0540\text{ mm}^2$.
  - Boot ROM: $0.0010\text{ mm}^2$.

---

- **Model Topology**: Time-domain conv/GRU + FFT-domain conv/GRU fused by 2 self-attention blocks and 1 cross-attention block.
- **Inference Latency on `clk_fast_i` (114 MHz)**:
  - CWRU Shipped Model (47,076 parameters): **46.7 ms** at 94–95% accuracy (INT8 = FP32).
  - Full AVIP Model (478,277 parameters): **54.5 ms** (10× parameters but only 1.2× compute).
- **Stator Current Signature Analysis (CSA)**:
  - Phase-current SAR ADC sampled at PWM ripple null detects mechanical bearing fault frequencies: $f_{\text{fault}} = f_e \pm k \cdot f_{\text{defect}}$.
  - **Eliminates external accelerometers and vibration probes entirely**, reusing the motor's own electrical sensing.

chunks.text:
India's aerospace and commercial robotics sectors currently import over 95% of tactical UAV flight controllers, ESC power stages, and navigation silicon—principally from STMicroelectronics (STM32 series), Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, and Chinese commercial autopilot suppliers. Under active Electronic Warfare (EW) conditions along contested borders (LoC and LAC), foreign commercial microcontrollers suffer from:
1. **Unverifiable Firmware & Supply Chain Kill-Switches**: Foreign proprietary IP blocks cannot be formally verified against side-channel Trojan insertion.
2. **GPS-Denial Catastrophic Drift**: Commercial flight stacks depend entirely on GNSS satellite signals. Under front-line jamming, positioning rapidly diverges, triggering unrecoverable airframe loss.
3. **Firmware Watchdog Lockup**: Software-managed task schedulers (e.g., in RTOS or Linux) can deadlock during RF desensitization or high-power thermal throttling, locking motor PWM channels in indeterminate states.

chunks.docTitle: Technical Annex v3 (10 SKUs, D100 & SDV)
chunks.text:
The **DeepGrid D100** is an integrated System-in-Package (SiP) specifically engineered to replace fragmented, imported multi-board avionics stacks with a single, sovereign 15x15 mm BGA package. It combines:
- **Dual DGridRiscV Flight Cores (RV32IM_Safety)** running deterministic, hard real-time PX4 / ArduPilot loops at 200 MHz fixed clock.
- **Hardware 6-DoF Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) VIO Engine** processing MIPI CSI-2 optical streams and IMU telemetry at 30 Hz with $<1\%$ drift per kilometer under zero-GNSS conditions.
- **Dedicated, 100% Isolated Hardware Failsafe Island**: Pure digital RTL state machine with isolated power and clock domains that bypasses the main processors and directly drives motor ESCs into a controlled recovery descent upon command link loss.
- **Heterogeneous Organic SiP Integration**: 6 wire-bonded mature-node dies (PMIC, Supervisor, Transceiver, Motor Driver, AFE) combined with high-speed compute on a 4-layer organic BGA substrate, **deliberately rejecting costly UCIe or silicon interposers**.

---

chunks.section: 2. Silicon Process Physics & Subsystem Die Allocation
chunks.text:
DeepGrid strictly enforces the **130nm Physics Boundary**: mature silicon handles high-voltage power conditioning, rugged analog signal acquisition, and ultra-high frequency RF, while high-density digital nodes are sequestered to isolated compute dies.

| Subsystem / Die | Node & Foundry | Key Technology & Physics | Target Socket / Function |
|---|---|---|---|

- **Instruction Set Architecture**: RV32IM_Zicsr (Standard 32-bit RISC-V integer arithmetic + hardware integer multiplier/divider).
- **Pipeline Structure**: 2-stage fetch / 6-stage execute deterministic pipeline.
- **Cacheless Microarchitecture**: To eliminate non-deterministic cache-miss jitter, the core executes code exclusively out of a **512 KB Zero-Wait-State Tightly-Coupled SRAM with Single-Error Correction Double-Error Detection (SECDED ECC)**.
- **Safety Redundancy**: Dual cores run in lockstep with a 2-cycle staggered temporal skew to prevent common-mode electrical transient faults. A hardware comparator triggers `FAULTn` within $\le 2$ clock cycles upon mismatch.

chunks.section: 3.2 30 Hz Hardware Geometric EKF VIO Engine
chunks.text:
In modern counter-UAS electronic warfare, GPS signals are spoofed or completely suppressed. The D100 implements pure geometric localization in hardware:
- **Optical Ingestion**: 2-lane MIPI CSI-2 interface ingesting 1080p60 grayscale optical tracking frames.
- **Hardware Image Signal Processor (ISP)**: On-the-fly debayering, high-dynamic-range (HDR) tone curve mapping, and FAST corner detector extracting up to 500 optical keypoints per frame.
- **Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)**: Hardwired matrix math accelerator solving 6-DoF pose equations (3-axis velocity, 3-axis orientation, accelerometer bias, gyro bias) at 30 Hz.
- **Drift Rate**: Geometric relative drift is constrained to **$<0.8\%$ of distance traveled**, enabling autonomous return-to-base without GPS or magnetic compass.

chunks.section: 3.3 The Hardware Failsafe Island (The Hardware Wedge)
chunks.text:
Unlike commercial flight controllers where failsafe procedures are executed by software routines (vulnerable to kernel panics, stack overflow, or memory corruption), the D100 implements a **100% physically isolated Failsafe Island**:
1. **Isolated Power & Clock Domain**: Powered by an independent internal low-dropout regulator (LDO) and driven by an on-chip ring oscillator decoupled from external crystals.
2. **Autonomous Hardware Link Monitor**: Directly samples RF telemetry packets, SBUS/CRSF receiver signals, and GNSS lock status. If loss-of-link persists beyond a programmable threshold (e.g., 500 ms), the island asserts state override.
3. **Emergency Safe-State FSM**: A pure combinational/synchronous finite state machine that calculates a steady-state rotor speed profile based on last-known altitude barometry.
4. **Hardwired Actuator Multiplexer (MUX)**: Positioned at the silicon I/O pad boundary. When activated, it **completely disconnects the main processors, VIO engine, and AI stack**, driving predictable recovery PWM/DShot signals directly to the motor ESCs.

```

| D100 SILICON I/O BOUNDARY                                                     |
|                                                                               |
| [Main Flight Processor] ---> (Normal PWM/DShot) ---+                          |
|                                                    |                          |
|                                             +------v-------+                  |
|                                             | HARDWARE MUX | ===> ESC MOTORS  |
|                                             +------^-------+                  |

Advanced chiplet packaging standards such as UCIe, TSMC CoWoS, or Intel EMIB require sub-micron silicon interposers, micro-bumps ($<40\ \mu\text{m}$ pitch), and access to offshore advanced packaging foundries. For sovereign Indian defence systems, this re-introduces the exact geopolitical vulnerability being avoided.

DeepGrid packages the D100 using a **standard 4-layer organic laminate substrate (FR4/BT core)**:
- **Package Dimensions**: $15 \times 15\text{ mm}$ Ball Grid Array (BGA), 0.8 mm ball pitch, 324-ball count.
- **Die Interconnect**: Mature dies (PMIC, Supervisor, Transceiver) are standard aluminum/gold wire-bonded ($25\ \mu\text{m}$ wire). The high-density compute die is flip-chip attached using copper pillar bumps ($100\ \mu\text{m}$ pitch).
- **Communication Protocol**: Inter-die communication utilizes standardized on-substrate routing buses: high-speed SPI, differential UART, and dedicated reset/interrupt GPIO lines.
- **Cost Impact**: Reduces packaging NRE from $>\$1.5\text{M}$ (silicon interposer) to $<\$35,000$ (organic substrate tooling), with high yield across domestic ATMP facilities.

chunks.section: DeepGrid Semi — DG32-LITE & DG32-2DOM Datasheet Engineering Specification
chunks.text:
**Document Classification:** Confidential Preliminary Datasheet Specification (CI2609 & CI2612 Releases)  
**Corporate Entity:** DeepGrid Semi Pvt Ltd · CIN: U62099TS2024PTC183631 · T-Hub Phase 2, Hyderabad  
**Package:** 64-pin QFN ($9.0 \times 9.0\ \text{mm}$, 0.5 mm pitch, exposed paddle = VSS)  
**Process Technology:** SkyWater sky130A (130 nm CMOS)  

---

DeepGrid Semi's motor-control silicon family comprises two primary silicon variants sharing a common physical footprint, pad ring, and register base:

1. **DG32-LITE (chipIgnite CI2609 Shuttle):**
   - Single 50 MHz clock domain.
   - Dual RV32IMC DGridRiscV cores in cycle-by-cycle hardware lockstep.
   - 32 KB on-chip SRAM (16x sky130 macros, parity-none), 64 KB baked boot ROM, QSPI-XIP external NOR flash window.
   - 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM with programmable dead-time, 4-channel DShot ESC engine (pad-muxed), quadrature + Hall encoder, CORDIC math unit, and on-die 8-bit differential SAR ADC.
   - Target power: ~0.43 W @ 50 MHz (tt 25 °C, 1.8 V core).

2. **DG32-2DOM (chipIgnite CI2612 Shuttle):**
   - Larger die ($3400 \times 4500\ \mu\text{m}$, $15.30\ \text{mm}^2$) accommodating the frozen lockstep motor-control core plus a hardware INT8 attention accelerator (`dgrid_int8_attn`).
   - Dual clock domains: 50 MHz CPU domain and 114 MHz fast domain (`clk_fast_i`), linked across 4-phase req/ack CDC bridges with 2-FF synchronizers.
   - Memory-mapped attention engine at `0xE000_0000`: executes full softmax, 256-entry u15 EXP table, and 40-bit accumulator numerator.
   - Identical external 64-pin QFN pinout: pin-compatible drop-in replacement for DG32-LITE carrier boards.

---

| Pin | Name | Type | Domain | Description & PCB Connection Rule |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **1** | `vssa2` | Ground | Ground | Analog substrate ground |
| **2** | `ADC_VINN` | Analog | 1.8V vccd1 | SAR ADC negative differential input (0 to 1.8 V) |
| **3** | `PWM_AH` | Output | 3.3V vddio | Phase A High-Side PWM gate drive / DShot CH0 |

- **Core Logic & SRAM (`vccd1`, pin 49):** 1.71 V to 1.89 V (Nominal: 1.8 V $\pm 5\%$).
- **Harness Core (`vccd`, pin 18):** 1.71 V to 1.89 V (Nominal: 1.8 V).
- **Pad Ring & ESD (`vddio`, pins 17, 64):** 3.0 V to 3.6 V (Nominal: 3.3 V $\pm 10\%$).
- **Harness Analog / POR (`vdda`, pin 30):** 3.0 V to 3.6 V (Nominal: 3.3 V).
- **Core Clock (`CLK`, pin 31):** 50 MHz design target ($f_{\max}$ post-route 55–62 MHz).
- **Differential ADC Input (`ADC_VINP`, `ADC_VINN`):** 0 to 1.8 V differential.

1. **Ramp Order:** Bring up 3.3 V (`vddio`, `vdda`) **before or coincident with** 1.8 V (`vccd`, `vccd1`).
2. **Voltage Differential:** At no point during power-up, steady-state, or power-down may `vccd1` exceed `vddio` by $>0.3\ \text{V}$.
3. **Unused Rail Biasing:** Unused rails (`vdda1`, `vdda2`, `vccd2`) must be tied to nominal voltages (3.3V and 1.8V) to ensure the pad ring's domain-order ESD steering diodes remain properly reversed-biased.
4. **Current Dissipation:** Dynamic and leakage current is drawn entirely from `vccd1` (~0.43 W at 50 MHz, tt 25 °C).

---

The SoC has no external management core. At power-on reset, the 64 KB baked std-cell boot ROM executes autonomously:
1. **UART Banner:** Emits `DG32` boot banner on `UART0_TX` (pin 42) at 115,200 baud, 8N1 (divider = 434 @ 50 MHz).
2. **QSPI Flash Detection:** Reads external NOR flash header through the `0x1000_0000` window:
   - Validates 32-bit boot magic word: `0xD632_B007`.
   - Reads 32-bit payload length word.
3. **Image Transfer:** Copies executable binary from NOR flash into 32 KB SRAM using QSPI quad-output-fast-read opcode `0x6B` (1-1-4 mode, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = 25 MHz).
4. **Execution Jump:** Branches execution to SRAM (`0x9000_0000`).
5. **Fallback:** If flash is blank or invalid, ROM drops to an interactive UART monitor (`r` read, `w` write, `j` jump, `i` info) so bare boards remain inspectable without JTAG.
